evidence.excerpt: In an allele name such as HLA-A*02:01:01:01 the fields carry distinct meanings (official HLA nomenclature). An optional suffix gives expression status: N for a null allele, and L, S, C, A or Q for alternatively expressed alleles, L meaning significantly reduced surface expression. A name without a suffix is not a measurement of how much HLA a cancer cell expresses. A shared first field does not establish identical proteins, and a report stating only A*02 at group resolution cannot be silently completed as A*02:01.

evidence.excerpt: Laboratory typing starts from an accepted specimen and extracted DNA, tests sequence patterns with primers or probes or reads selected regions by Sanger or next-generation sequencing, optionally after PCR amplification, and compares the result with a reference database (IPD-IMGT/HLA). Hosomichi et al. (2013) describe phase-defined sequencing of six HLA genes by long-range PCR and multiplex sequencing: phasing connects differences on the same inherited copy, and unresolved phase or a missing distinguishing region can leave alternative allele pairs despite good base quality. More reads of the same regions cannot settle such an ambiguity; the distinguishing information must be added, and both alternatives should be kept until it is. Software can infer class I HLA from genome, exome or RNA sequencing: Szolek et al. (2014) reported OptiType's overall accuracy of 97 per cent on their benchmark of RNA, exome and whole-genome data. Capture, coverage and expression affect such inference, and an inference is not automatically a laboratory result accepted for clinical use. Reports should be read with resolution, ambiguity notes, coverage, database version and validation.

evidence.excerpt: People generally inherit one copy of each HLA gene from each parent, so a report lists two alleles per locus, which can be the same name. Class I and class II typing describe different display molecules. Typing identifies inheritance; it does not show tumour retention or expression, peptide display or receptor recognition, and a negative display assay does not by itself show the typing was wrong. Loss of an allele in the tumour, or changes in antigen-processing machinery, can interrupt the chain after an accurate typing result. A trial may name an allele and an accepted method; eligibility belongs to the study team and neither a similar name nor correct typing shows targetability.

Tissue distribution, persistence, safety and clinical benefit still need their own evidence. A suitable clinical comparison estimates benefit for that population, product and setting, without automatic transfer elsewhere.

rows.requirement: Proteasome cutting, TAP transport and ERAP trimming shape fragments; trimming can generate or destroy an epitope and more encoded windows do not bypass a shared processing defect.

evidence.excerpt: Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

evidence.excerpt: NetMHCpan-4.0 combined peptide-binding affinity data with eluted-ligand data, which also contain information about processing and natural presentation. Those training signals and prediction tasks should be distinguished. A consortium comparison assessed candidate tumor epitopes using measured immune interactions and developed improved prioritization features. A model score is a prediction with a validation setting; it is not an observation of peptide display, tumor recognition or patient benefit. The NetMHCpan-4.1 documentation expresses binder thresholds as percentile rank, the position of a predicted score against the scores of random natural peptides, and lets the user set the strong and weak binder thresholds, so a 0.4 per cent rank places a candidate within the top 0.4 per cent of that reference and is not a 99.6 per cent probability of presentation, recognition or benefit. The server predicts binding of a peptide to an MHC molecule of known sequence, and its model is trained on more than 850,000 binding-affinity and mass-spectrometry eluted-ligand peptides, two different training signals (Reynisson and colleagues, 2020). A model trained on more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 single-allele cell lines improved prediction of presented peptides (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). In a consortium study, 608 predicted epitopes were then tested for T-cell binding in patient-matched samples, a separate experiment from the prediction (Wells and colleagues, 2020), so expression, processing, display, T-cell receptor recognition and sparing of healthy tissue remain to be shown after a favourable score.

Assay distinction. A predicted binding IC50 estimates a competitive-binding assay endpoint. An IC50 depends on the assay conditions and is not automatically an equilibrium dissociation constant. Cer and colleagues' 2009 IC50-to-Ki tool calculates binding or inhibition constants using the interaction mechanism, concentrations and other assumptions; this is a biochemical distinction, not validation of an HLA model or a measure of cancer-cell growth inhibition. Reading guide (OnCo inference): Record the model and version, allele, peptide length, prediction task, units, reference distribution and threshold beside every score, and do not put a rank and an IC50 in one unlabelled column. A threshold is a selection rule for a stated workflow and cannot repair the wrong allele or an unsupported task. Inputs are peptide or source-protein sequences and an exact allele; scoring uses no tumour tissue; held-out validation, allele coverage and the endpoint (binding, recovery or T-cell recognition) decide what a good score means.

evidence.excerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

Receptor sequencing asks which receptor sequences are represented and in what relative abundance. ELISpot asks how many input cells release the chosen molecule under the stated stimulation. An expanded sequence does not establish that it caused a spot, and a spot in mixed cells does not identify a receptor sequence. Connecting identity to recognition or killing requires additional experiments with suitable controls.

evidence.excerpt: A primary flow-cytometry method distinguished labeled target cells from immune effector cells and measured target death while characterizing the effector population. The study examined how timing and the effector-to-target ratio affected the assay. Degranulation markers provide a related functional readout, but they measure a step preceding cytolysis. Killing of a laboratory target does not establish recognition of every tumor cell or benefit in the person receiving a treatment.

Scope of the methods: a flow-based assay labels targets with a dye, adds a dead-cell stain and analyses released nuclei, which lowers errors from target-effector aggregates, and it reported four nuclear staining patterns separating target and effector nuclei and live and dead cells (Rabinovich 2019). Degranulation (CD107 exposure) preceded cytolysis and was concordant with interferon gamma in the original report, and is distinct from completed target death (Betts 2003). Model-specific killing does not show trafficking, persistence, healthy-tissue safety or patient benefit.

Method card, what it measures: binding of cells to a specified peptide held by a specified HLA allele, under the staining conditions. How: HLA molecules are assembled with the selected peptide and several copies are attached to a labelled scaffold (a tetramer is one format), cells are exposed and analysed, usually by flow cytometry, with viable-cell and gate selection. Failure modes: nonspecific binding, weak binding, dead cells, a wrong or poorly formed reagent, chain differences or sampling loss. evidence.excerpt: The National Library of Medicine distinguishes mononuclear leukocytes from granulocytes and from monocytes alone. A primary study of immune monitoring in HIV vaccine research found that processing and cryopreservation conditions affected cell recovery, viability and measured antigen responses. What the fraction is: peripheral blood mononuclear cells are circulating white blood cells with a single unsegmented nucleus, mainly lymphocytes and monocytes, with T, B and natural killer cells among them, isolated by layering anticoagulated blood over a density-separation medium and collecting the interface. Most conventional granulocytes and red cells separate elsewhere, but recovery is incomplete, so platelets, red cells or low-density granulocytes can contaminate a preparation, and the label PBMC does not guarantee purity. The classic density-gradient method dates from 1968 (Boyum 1968). Isolation selects a recoverable blood fraction and does not sample tumour or give a complete immune census.

evidence.excerpt: The immunopeptidome is a biological repertoire in a defined cell population and context; an immunopeptidomics list is a method-dependent subset recovered and identified from a sample. A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019).
